articles.title: Bitter and sweet: on FSSAI draft restrictions, added sugars in infant foods
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The Food Safety and Standards Regulations 2020 currently allow manufacturers to add sucrose and fructose, provided their combined total does not exceed 20% of the carbohydrates in a product intended for infants aged 0-6 months. In a draft proposal, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has pitched to eliminate this allowance — in line with WHO’s recommendation to have infants breastfeed exclusively for the first six months, followed by nutritionally adequate complementary foods avoiding added sugars until 24 months. While corporations have defended sugary formulations as abiding by the Codex Alimentarius, public health experts have repeatedly described their decision to sell infant foods with added sugar as nutritional dumping. Adding sugar has often been a commercial strategy, as it serves as a cheap bulking agent, improves palatability and encourages repeat purchases. WHO’s nutrient and promotion profile model for baby foods in 2022 also identified sweet purées and products in which fruits released sugars during processing as concerns. While the FSSAI’s draft proposal is a step in the right direction, stopping here would allow manufacturers to replace sucrose with another sweetening ingredient. It should assess the ingredients that manufacturers add and the nutritional profile of the finished food, thus completing the loop, with the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles, and Infant Foods Act 1992 rightly restricting aggressively the marketing of infant foods for children up to two years old.

Research has found that children who regularly received sweetened water during infancy subsequently preferred sweeter liquids, while exposure to different infant formula flavours influenced their dietary preferences years later, including for foods tasting neutral or bitter. Across both personal and public health dimensions, then, infants need to encounter diverse flavours. Since the 2024 dietary guidelines of the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition say that children under two should avoid added sugars, the FSSAI’s draft proposal limiting itself to six months seems like a concession to manufacturers. This should be avoided since India’s regulatory response to ultra-processed foods is expanding after years of sluggishness. India is currently mulling restrictions on added sugar in foods for the youngest infants, on unhealthy foods around schools, and on front-of-pack labelling for packaged foods. If the FSSAI does not expand its proposed restriction to cover all added sugars and extend it across the first 24 months, and pair it with mandatory, interpretative front-of-pack labelling for all foods, its regulatory progress will remain incomplete.

articles.title: ISKCON unveils 800-kg robotic elephant in Visakhapatnam
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: A moving robotic elephant named Ranga, weighing 800 kg, was unveiled on Sunday at MGM Park on Beach Road in front of a large gathering of devotees during ISKCON Visakhapatnam’s Sharad Purnima celebrations. The organisers described it as the first-of-its-kind in Andhra Pradesh.

ISKCON Governing Body chairman Madhusevita Prabhu inaugurated the elephant. Branch president Samba Das Prabhu and Nitai Sevini Mataji led the programme. According to ISKCON, the elephant was brought from Thrissur in Kerala and donated by PETA India.
A ‘Nauka Vihar’ (boat festival), Bhajan Clubbing and the ‘Kartika Deepotsavam’ followed ‘sankirtan’ of the Hare Krishna Maha Mantra.

CMR Group managing director Mavuri Venkata Ramana, Andhra University former Vice-Chancellor G.S.N. Raju, Simhachalam Devasthanam chief priest G. Srinivasacharyulu, and Pydah Educational Institutions chairman Pydah Krishna Prasad were also present on the ocassion.

articles.title: Bhavani devotees throng Kanaka Durga temple atop Indrakeeladri
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Sri Durga Malleswara Swamy Varla Devasthanam, abode of Goddess Kanaka Durga, atop Indrakeeladri, witnessed a massive influx of Bhavani devotees and general pilgrims from the early hours of Sunday (October 25, 2026), with thousands arriving from far-flung places to conclude their Bhavani Deeksha.
The hill shrine was filled with devotees dressed in red, while chants of “Jai Bhavani” reverberated across the temple premises, creating a spiritually charged atmosphere.
The rush began early in the morning, with devotees arriving from both the Ghat Road and Kanaka Durga Nagar routes. The queues grew crowded as the number of pilgrims continued to swell.
In view of the heavy rush, the temple administration introduced several measures to regulate the crowd and facilitate faster darshan for Bhavani devotees and general pilgrims.

As part of these arrangements, Antaralaya Darshan, which allows devotees to enter the inner sanctum, was completely suspended from the morning. Later, following the offering of Maha Nivedana to the presiding deity at noon, the temple authorities cancelled all categories of special-entry darshan tickets as well.

Consequently, only free Sarva Darshan was being permitted, allowing devotees waiting in the queues to have the darshan of Sri Kanaka Durga Devi without purchasing special-entry tickets. The move was aimed at improving the flow of pilgrims and providing greater access to ordinary devotees amid the unprecedented rush.

Temple officials were closely monitoring arrangements to ensure uninterrupted distribution of drinking water to pilgrims waiting in the queues and to prevent inconvenience during the prolonged waiting periods.

Temple Executive Officer V.K. Seena Naik appealed to the devotees to cooperate with the temple staff and security personnel, maintain discipline and follow the prescribed arrangements to ensure a smooth and orderly darshan of the Goddess.

articles.title: Officials urged to remain alert as severe cyclone approaches
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Krishna District Collector D.K. Balaji has directed officials to remain alert for the cyclone and take steps to prevent human and property loss.

Mr. Balaji, who reviewed cyclone preparedness with the district and mandal-level officials, instructed them to be available at the posted places and take measures for supply of drinking water and other essentials.

Meanwhile, Andhra Pradesh Central Power Distribution Corporation Limited (APCPDCL) CMD P. Pulla Reddy said leaves of officials and staff were cancelled in wake of the cyclonic storm. He also asked the field staff to caution the public against touching snapped electric cables. Control Rooms have been set up in all districts under CPDCL, Mr. Pulla Reddy said.
Eluru District Collector K. Vetri Selvi has directed the officials to be alert and asked the Irrigation department engineers to take measures to prevent damage to canal and tank bunds.
Villagers were requested not to venture into rivers and canals and move on the bunds as the impact of the cyclone would be heavy.

Control Rooms have been set up at Eluru Collectorate with helpline numbers 18002331077, 08812-224519 and 9491041419, and public are requested to contact and alert the officers in emergency, the Collector said.

NTR District Collector G. Lakshmisha reviewed the preparedness for the severe cyclone with the officials of Revenue, Irrigation, A.P. Transco, Medical and Health, Fire and other departments. He directed the Tahsildars to shift people staying in vulnerable areas to safer locations.
A control room has been set up the Collectorate with the helpline number 91549 70454 in Vijayawada, Mr. Lakshmisha said.
He appealed to the public not to take shelter in dilapidated buildings, under the trees, electric poles and hoardings during the event of the cyclone.

articles.title: Three North Andhra districts step up cyclone preparedness
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The administrations of Visakhapatnam, Anakapalli and Alluri Sitharama Raju (ASR) districts have stepped up preparedness on Sunday by setting up control rooms and readying relief centres, as a deep depression over the Bay of Bengal is expected to intensify into a cyclone, according to the India Meteorological Department.

Visakhapatnam Collector M. Abhishikth Kishore, reviewing arrangements at a videoconference with Greater Visakhapatnam Municipal Corporation (GVMC) Commissioner Ketan Garg said the impact could be as severe as that of Cyclone Montha . He directed officers to remain at their places of work.
A control room has been set up at the Collectorate, with others planned to be opened at the GVMC office and at zonal and mandal levels.
Officials were instructed to monitor reservoir levels, alert residents living on hill slopes and keep relief centres ready.
Mr. Garg said that people had earlier been evacuated from seven areas. The Collector directed officials to arrange for the shifting of those residents again.
Tree-cutting machines are to be stationed in advance, while the GVMC and APEPDCL were asked to ensure uninterrupted power supply.
Fishing boats on the beach at Pedda Jalaripeta in Visakhapatnam on Sunday, ahead of the forecast cyclonic storm. | Photo Credit: V RAJU

Ambulances, medical teams and medicines are to be kept ready. Pregnant women nearing delivery are to be moved to hospitals. Fishermen have been advised not to venture into the sea and, tourists and residents were warned against visiting beaches.

Special officers have been appointed for each constituency and mandal. The round-the-clock Collectorate control room can be reached on 0891-2590100 and 0891-2590102, said Special Deputy Collector and District Project Manager T. Govindu.
In Anakapalli, Collector Vijaya Krishnan said that people of low-lying and coastal areas were to be identified and relocated by the evening of October 26.
Relief centres would provide drinking water and food, while medicines would be available for patients with chronic ailments. High-risk pregnant women are to be shifted to health centres.

A round-the-clock control room will function at the Collectorate from October 26. Tahsildars and Mandal Parishad Development Officers have been directed to remain stationed at headquarters, with no leave granted.

articles.title: Jamia students climb gates, join protest amid heavy police deployment
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: A day after attempts were made to forcibly remove protesting students at Jamia Millia Islamia university, students gathered around the campus and tried to enter by climbing the gates on Sunday (October 25, 2026). With classes suspended, water facilities on the campus were cut off and no entry or exit was allowed. Amid heavy police deployment, students still gathered in large numbers and staged a protest.

On Saturday (October 24), security personnel, teaching and non-teaching staff attempted to remove the students protesting since October 11 for restoration of their students’ union. The tent was uprooted from the lawn inside gate no. 7, campus electricity and water facilities suspended, gates and libraries closed and all classes announced to be conducted online until further notice.

Following this, students gathered in large numbers and stayed through the night, singing songs, raising slogans and demanding the restoration of JMISU. On Sunday (October 25), a similar scenario was observed, with heavy CRPF and Delhi Police personnel guarding the entry gates and dispersing the students who were trying to enter.

“We have been trying to go inside the campus but the security personnel are not allowing us. They have barricaded gate no. 7 and no entry is allowed from other gates as well. In the afternoon, some students from the hostel tried to access the health centre from gate no. 4 but were not allowed,” said Md. Zubair, a second year Bachelor’s student.

With entry and exit banned, students inside the campus were unable to access filtered water, had to rely on friends to get water for them. Some students wanting to join the protest also climbed gates and entered. Delhi Police personnel stopped many students from entering by pulling and physically handling them. Some students were also detained.

Around 1:00 p.m., the Vice-Chancellor, along with administration and other staff, visited the campus, inspected the gates and security arrangements and left without interacting with the students. “We have been demanding a dialogue with the V-C and the Chief Proctor on the restoration of JMISU that has been non-existent since 2006. After inviting students for a dialogue, the V-C used force to remove us and end our protest,” alleged Habeeba, one of the students removed from the hostel.

An FIR has been registered under the charges of trespassing, defacement of property and confinement against political leaders and students following a complaint sent by Jamia administration, the police officials said.

The complaint was sent by the Economics department mentioning trespassing and damage to public property. “The complaint contains names of MPs, leaders, students and ex-students who were trying to trespass on campus property. The FIR has been registered under the charges of criminal trespassing, wrongful confinement and voluntarily causing hurt under BNS. We have also added Sections from Delhi Prevention of Defacement of Property Act, as per the complaint,” Additional Deputy Commissioner of Police, South East, said.

Three persons including two women were detained from outside the campus on Sunday. “The two women were not connected with Jamia at all. They were neither students, nor ex-students or associated with any student party or union. They were creating law and order problems and were detained. They were released before sunset,” the officer said.

“Another person was held under Preventive Detention. The man works with a food delivery app and is educated only till class 10. We found his activities suspicious and are currently questioning him for his purpose of being at the site. We will present him before the SEM tomorrow,” the officer added.

Students were informally being told to vacate the hostel on account of online classes and upcoming festivals. “The campus has moved online. There is no reason for anyone to stay on campus. They are also being asked to vacate informally as it is the festive season and parents like to see them at home,” an official from the Jamia administration said.

“Dialogue has been happening since day one. On Saturday (October 24), the entire Jamia, including professors, the administration and even the non-teaching staff, went to meet the students, but they did not want to end their protest,” the official said. On being asked why the students were forcibly removed, the official said, “If they had been removed, they would not have been there still.”

articles.title: Like Kerala, T.N. government should pass resolution in State Assembly to scrap SIR, says CPI (M) politburo member
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Communist Party of India (Marxist) politburo member G. Ramakrishnan on Sunday said that Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) president and Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay should introduce and adopt a resolution in the State Legislative Assembly to scrap the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.

Addressing reporters after participating in a free medical camp for construction workers in Vellore town, Mr. Ramakrishnan alleged that the BJP-led Union government has used SIR to delete around 13.5 crore voters from the electoral rolls in the country. In this regard, except BJP, the entire opposition have united in demanding the removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. “On its part, the Tamil Nadu government led by Mr. Vijay should pass a resolution against SIR in the State Assembly and for re-enrolment of voters, who were deleted from the electoral rolls,” he said.

The CPI (M) leader cited the example of Kerala Legislative Assembly, where the ruling Congress and Opposition parties led by the Left Front have unanimously passed a resolution, demanding the scrapping of SIR of electoral rolls.

articles.title: Venezuela's Opposition leader Machado returns after months in exile, as doubts over democracy deepen
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Opposition leader and Nobel laureate Maria Corina Machado reappeared in Venezuela on Sunday (October 25, 2026) for the first time since December, returning from exile at a time when doubts about the country's democratic future — and the role of the U.S. —are growing.

It was her first appearance since the U.S. military deposed the country's then-President Nicolás Maduro, replacing him with an interim president who has exceeded the time she was authorised to serve, with no election scheduled.
Ms. Machado announced her arrival on social media, writing, “I am here. With you.”
Another leading figure in the Venezuelan opposition, Edmundo González, wrote on X confirming that Ms. Machado had arrived and that he would be next to her “very soon.”
“Today is a very important day for Venezuelans. Our sovereign voice returns with her to lead and guide this process!” he wrote. “You know it, this is until the end.”

On Sunday afternoon (October 25, 2026), Ms. Machado strode into a church in the town of Lara, west of Caracas, to the applause of dozens gathered there as they shook her hand and hugged her, with cell phones aloft to record her return. “Maria! Maria!” someone cried out.

Asked by reporters on Sunday (October 25, 2026) about Ms. Machado's return to Venezuela, U.S. President Donald Trump said, “I don't know anything about it, but I think she's a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel Prize. So how can I say anything else? And I hope she's safe. She's a very nice woman. But we're doing really well in Venezuela.”
Since Mr. Maduro's ouster, Venezuela has been run by acting President Delcy Rodriguez, a longtime Maduro ally who received the Trump administration's blessing to succeed him.
Ms. Rodriguez was initially supposed to serve only 90 days as acting president, but has remained in office and has made no move to call an election.

Ms. Machado was briefly detained in January 2025, following a protest against Mr. Maduro's planned swearing-in ceremony, and went into hiding in Venezuela for 11 months. After making a clandestine escape from the country, she reappeared that December in Norway, where she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her peaceful challenge to Mr. Maduro's authoritarian government.
Ms. Machado and her allies have been demanding a date for a presidential election in Venezuela, but U.S. officials have emphasized economic stabilization first.
In October 2023, Ms. Machado won an opposition primary and intended to challenge Mr. Maduro in the 2024 presidential election, but the government barred her from running for office.

articles.title: U.K. PM Burnham says he is open to discussing EU free movement
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: British Prime Minister ​Andy Burnham has said he wants a discussion about returning to ⁠the European Union’s freedom of movement rules for workers, a key issue in the 2016 Brexit referendum which led to Britain leaving the bloc.

Building on previous comments about the need to ‌rethink ties with Brussels, Mr. Burnham told the Sunday Times that the influx of EU workers into Britain before Brexit had posed very ‌significant challenges. “But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that ‌perhaps ⁠wasn’t as difficult (as now),” he said.

“Revolving door migration where people would ⁠come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”
Official data has shown ​long-term net migration in 2025 ‌fell to close to its level before a new post-Brexit immigration system was introduced at the start of 2021.

In September, two months after replacing Keir Starmer as Labour Party leader and prime minister, Mr. Burnham said Britain should consider options ‌for its relationship with the EU, including possibly rejoining the bloc one ​day.
He had previously backed the pledges of Starmer’s government which included no return to freedom of movement which Brussels sets as a ⁠condition for being part of the bloc’s single market.

In his interview with the Sunday Times , conducted on October 19, Mr. Burnham said the issue of freedom of ‌movement could be considered as part of a broader reset of Britain’s relationship with the EU, including on data sharing and migration. “You’ve got to see it in the round, rather than just looking at freedom of movement on its own,” he said.
Mr. Burnham — who is trying to find ways to speed up Britain’s economy is due to meet top EU officials for a summit on November 20.
He ‌said he could not imagine recommending that Britain adopt the euro currency or the EU’s border-free ​travel arrangements.
A new referendum would be needed to rejoin the EU but not necessarily to join the bloc’s single market or ⁠a customs union, the Sunday Times quoted Mr. Burnham as saying.

Former Conservative finance minister Jeremy ⁠Hunt, who campaigned to stay in the EU in 2016, said it would be a mistake to reopen one of the fundamental debates of ‌the referendum and he said relaxing immigration rules would hurt people in Britain. “I think it will be a hammer blow to getting people off welfare ​and into work,” he told Sky News.

articles.title: Beyond national interest: role of ethics and emotions in world politics
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: The language of world politics has become remarkably predictable. Every military strike, diplomatic initiative, economic sanction, or strategic partnership is justified in the name of national interest. Television debates and commentaries have a common vocabulary — power, deterrence, balance of power, strategic autonomy, and security. It almost appears as though International Relations has become an emotionless discipline, focused on power concentration, where morality and ethics have little place. Yet the defining geopolitical crises of recent years tell a very different story.

International Relations, both as an academic discipline and as a practice of diplomacy, has been largely shaped by Western intellectual traditions, with much of academic research originating in the United States of America. No wonder, famous IR scholar, Stanley Hoffman, in his article, argued that IR is an American Social Science. It is difficult to refute Hoffman’s argument because initially the modern international order emerged when European powers dominated much of the world, leaving the Global South with little role in designing the institutions, norms, and rules that continue to govern global politics. However, the discipline itself acquired its modern identity after the Second World War, with the U.S. based scholar, Hans Morgenthau’s Realism becoming the dominant framework for understanding international affairs. Realism portrays the international system as anarchic and argues that states, in the absence of a central authority, are compelled to pursue their national interests. Although the theory is far more nuanced than its popular interpretation suggests, public discourse has reduced it to two defining ideas—anarchy and national interest. Over time, Realism travelled from classrooms to newsrooms, becoming the default language through which foreign policy is interpreted.

articles.title: UPI and the cost of policy reversal
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The government has just given itself the legal room to tax the very payment habit it spent a decade building. Tucked into the Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026, is an amendment to Section 10A of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, which would allow the government to notify charges on specified electronic payment modes. The number being proposed is a Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) of 0.25–0.5% on UPI transactions above ₹2,000. The official stand is that this threshold would touch only about five per cent of transactions by volume, sparing the milk-and-vegetable payments that make up the bulk of UPI’s use. But it would cover roughly 65% of transaction value, which is precisely why it matters.
This is not a small, technical fix. It runs counter to a decade-long policy commitment and deserves more scrutiny than it has received.

Consider the arc. Demonetisation in November 2016 was justified, among other things, as a push towards a less-cash economy. UPI, launched earlier that year, became the vehicle for that push, and its zero-MDR regime was a deliberate subsidy to get merchants and consumers off cash. It worked spectacularly. UPI now processes more transactions each month than most of the world’s card networks combined. Having successfully weaned the country away from cash and towards electronic payments, the government now wants to undercut the very success it engineered.

There seems to be a continued pattern of privileging one payment mode over others via policy. India has long taxed even credit cards. Credit card interest and fees attract 18% GST, making the use of credit cards unnecessarily costly. Taxing interest on revolving credit is unusual by international standards; most jurisdictions treat consumer credit interest as a private financial cost, not a taxable service. India taxes it as if using a credit card itself is a luxury.

Now UPI, the payment rail the government spent political capital promoting, is in line for similar treatment. The pattern suggests a need for a more coherent payments policy than giving in to the temptation to tax every transaction that can be observed.
There are at least two problems with this specific move beyond the optics.

First, basic economic theory tells us that the person on whom a tax is levied and the person who actually bears its cost are not always the same. Moreover, UPI or any payments interface is a two-sided market, and taxing two-sided markets is genuinely tricky.

The MDR would nominally fall on merchants, as argued by the government, collected via banks and the National Payments Corporation of India’s ecosystem. But whether that cost gets passed through to merchants, on to consumers, or absorbed by banks and payment service providers depends on competitive intensity on each side of the market. Banks and fintechs compete for merchant relationships and cannot easily raise prices without losing volume to a rival offering free UPI acceptance.

The more likely outcome is that intermediaries — the banks and PSPs that built and maintain the plumbing — absorb the cost, which erodes their incentive to invest in reliability, fraud prevention and expansion into underserved segments. A tax that cannot be reliably passed through does not disappear; it most likely shows up later as degraded service or slower innovation. This is completely counterintuitive if government is proposing this tax as necessary to fund the next stage of UPI growth.

Second, UPI has done real work on financial inclusion at the margin. It has pulled informal transactions into a recorded, traceable digital trail — the very outcome that formalisation and tax-compliance advocates have wanted for years. There have also been attempts to provide credit based on the digital trail created by electronic payments. Every rupee that moves through UPI instead of cash is a rupee the financial institutions can eventually see and use to build a spending profile.

Charging the rail directly could undercut the incentive to use it, cutting against long-standing financial inclusion goals. The government does not need to raise revenue from every rupee that moves electronically; it needs those rupees to keep moving electronically, because that is what delivers the inclusion and compliance dividends it has been chasing since 2016.

Ideally, which payment mode to adopt should be an economic decision for participating actors. Factors such as the size of the business, consumer preferences, and relative cost of using alternative payment systems should determine their usage. Deliberate policy intervention and the current government’s war on cash tilted the scales in favour of UPI. Taxing it now — however nominal or small — could change its usage patterns, and policymakers should not be surprised if one outcome is reduced UPI usage.

articles.title: How India’s life insurance sector funds government expenditure
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: When the government borrows, the question that follows is rarely asked aloud: who lends? A large part of the answer is the life insurance sector. Every year, millions of households across India pay premiums into life insurance policies. That money is reinvested, for decades, in the very securities that finance government expenditure — roads, railways, water supplies, hospitals, defence. The household protecting itself against the loss of its breadwinner is simultaneously, and unknowingly, lending to the sovereign [the Central government]. Life insurers collectively hold close to a quarter of India’s outstanding central government dated securities, based on RBI and IRDAI data — a share that has remained stable even as the total sovereign debt stock expanded by around 40 per cent in three years. This is not a number that appears in budget speeches or parliamentary debates. It is, however, a number that matters.

The stoic and resilient quality of the sector’s sovereign support is as significant as its scale. Life insurers write policies with tenures of twenty, thirty, sometimes forty years. Government securities are the natural habitat of long-duration liabilities — the only asset class that absorbs this scale of funds at matching tenures without distorting the market. Unlike foreign portfolio investors, whose appetite fluctuates with global risk sentiment, insurance companies buy and hold. They do not exit when oil prices rise or when a geopolitical event triggers a reassessment of emerging market exposure. Their participation is counter-cyclical by design — stable precisely when other buyers become unreliable. A steady domestic base of long-horizon holders reduces rollover risk and moderates borrowing costs across the maturity spectrum.
Life insurers buy when others sell, hold when others exit, and reinvest when others pause. That is the structural consequence of writing long-duration promises to millions of policyholders.

The sector’s contribution is not evenly distributed. The Life Insurance Corporation of India carries the dominant share — a consequence of its scale, its predominantly participating product mix, and the duration of its in-force book. Its March 2025 regulatory filing with IRDAI (Form L-26) confirms that sovereign paper accounts for nearly 63 per cent of its non-linked policyholder corpus — well above the regulatory minimum, and a direct expression of what long-duration liabilities demand at scale.

LIC holds approximately 19 per cent of all outstanding central government dated securities — a figure confirmed by the RBI’s Public Debt Management Quarterly Report for FY24, the most recently published data. LIC’s IRDAI regulatory filings for March 2025 give the institutional reality in absolute terms: ₹20.2 lakh crore in central government securities alone, and ₹32.3 lakh crore in total government and government-guaranteed securities across all funds. These are not estimates. They are figures LIC files with its regulator every quarter and that any researcher can access on the IRDAI website. This makes LIC the single largest institutional holder of Indian government’s debt.
Government securities are the natural habitat of long-duration liabilities — the only asset class that absorbs this scale of funds at matching tenures without distorting the market.

Private life insurers, with a higher proportion of unit-linked and shorter-tenure products, contribute a smaller fraction today. As they grow and deepen their traditional offerings, their sovereign allocations will follow the same structural logic.

The regulator has already recognised the systemic dimension of this function: IRDAI designates LIC as a Domestic Systemically Important Insurer every year, describing it as an institution whose distress would cause significant dislocation in the financial system. That designation, rightly made on insurance-sector grounds, points toward a wider truth — the dislocation would extend into the sovereign borrowing programme itself.

Insurers in Japan, the United Kingdom, and South Korea are among the largest holders of their respective governments’ long-dated securities, not because regulation mandates it but because their liability profiles demand it. India’s life insurance sector is following the same path.

India’s life insurance penetration stood at 2.7 per cent of GDP in FY25, the third consecutive year of decline from a pandemic-era peak of 3.2 per cent, against a global life average of 3.0 per cent. Three regulatory interventions between 2023 and 2024 — restructured distribution economics, taxation on certain high-value policies, and mandatory product repricing, simultaneously, has compressed new businesses. While each was defensible in isolation, their cumulative effect was adverse. The sector is recovering. But the episode illustrates a risk worth noting: when multiple regulatory actions compress new business at once, the household savings that would otherwise have flowed into the sovereign debt market through insurance, reduce or find shorter-duration homes elsewhere. The sovereign borrowing programme may not notice this in the short term. Over a decade, it would.
Banking commands policy attention in proportion to its systemic importance. Insurance, which quietly holds close to a quarter of outstanding central government dated securities, does not.

The case for deeper insurance penetration is most often made in the language of household financial protection — the uninsured family, the inadequate sum assured, a mis-sold product or an unsettled claim. These are legitimate concerns. But there is a parallel case, made in the language of sovereign fiscal stability, that has not been fully articulated in public policy discourse. If the reliability of India’s domestic sovereign funding base is a macroeconomic priority given the scale of annual borrowing requirements, then the depth and health of the life insurance sector remain directly relevant to that priority.

articles.title: Swiping in dark: The hidden cost of plastic money
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: A smartwatch bought on impulse, a costly phone ordered just for the thrill of owning it, a festive sale too tempting to resist. In isolation, each swipe may seem harmless, yet the danger lies in accumulation. Money spent in moments of desire can quietly turn into a burden that outlasts the fleeting gratification. Small indulgences, if they add up to a sizeable bill, can take a toll on the monthly budget and derail carefully planned financial goals.
The litmus test comes knocking much later, after the swipes have ended: a shocking bill. Now, to overcome the shock, cardholders often look for a shortcut: paying just the minimum due.

The minimum-due loop is one of the most deceptive traps of a credit card. Paying only this negligible fraction may help avert immediate late-payment penalties and default notices. However, it allows the bulk of your debt to linger and compound.

Crucially, carrying a due attracts interest and simultaneously revokes the interest-free grace period for subsequent purchases. Any new spend begins accruing interest charges immediately at typical annual rates of 36% to 42%, compounded monthly, until the entire bill is cleared in full. If the minimum-due route is a slow leak, ignoring the bill payment entirely is an outright rupture. Failing to pay the minimum due carries far more severe consequences.

The bank would immediately flag the account as overdue, levying hefty late-payment penalties on top of the standard charges. If the default crosses a stipulated time, the bank reports the delinquency to CIBIL and other credit bureaus, leaving a long-lasting scar on your score.

When the bill is bulky, cardholders often lean towards another tempting escape hatch: easy EMIs. Converting a purchase into equated monthly instalments does not erase the cost; rather, it locks you into a high-margin contract.
You forfeit the upfront discounts that are often bundled with full payment, while a relentless 18% GST is slapped onto the interest portion of every single EMI.
By splitting past impulse purchases across future months, you silently mortgage your upcoming cash flows. The bitter truth: the thrill of owning fades fast, but the bill of burden goes on and on.

Paying your bill on time is only half the battle. Even if you are punctual in clearing the bills, it’s not a total financial hygiene. When the usage on your card is close to its ceiling, you trigger an alarm button inside credit bureaus. Lenders gauge your financial stability through credit utilisation, and crossing the 30% threshold paints a picture of being cash hungry. Even if you do not default payment, a high usage of credit erodes your CIBIL score rating, transforming routine swipes into a hidden roadblock when you eventually apply for a home or vehicle loan.
Gliding your credit card smoothly into an ATM for quick cash would force you to endure a rough patch with huge money leaks.

On most credit cards, cash withdrawals carry zero grace period, meaning standard interest rates of 36 to 42% begin compounding moments after the currency is dispensed. Even on select promotional cards that tout an interest-free window, the fixed fees bite hard.

For instance, banks usually cap single ATM withdrawals at ₹10,000 while levying a flat processing fee of around ₹199 plus GST on every single attempt. Therefore, a requirement of ₹50,000 forces you to glide into the vending tunnel five times, instantly draining roughly over ₹1,000 in raw processing charges alone.

articles.title: A blueprint for India’s next energy transition: to electrify industrial heat
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: I ndia’s energy transition is already mainstreaming renewable-powered electrification across major demand centres. Electric mobility is replacing internal combustion engines, agriculture is increasingly powered by solar irrigation, and buildings are adopting smarter appliances. The next phase lies in electrifying industrial heat, particularly across India’s MSMEs, to strengthen manufacturing competitiveness, energy security and decarbonisation.

India’s solar photovoltaic revolution reduced solar tariffs by more than 85% over the past decade through a coordinated ecosystem of supportive policies both at the national and state level, innovative financing, competitive vendors and markets, institutional mandates, and sustained private sector investment. Now, scaling industrial heat electrification will require a similar approach. The focus has shifted to how India plans and scales this transition.

articles.title: Ethanol tender sparks feedstock concerns as rice gains ground over maize
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The Oil Marketing Companies’ (OMCs) latest ethanol procurement tender for Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) 2026–27 has triggered concerns among grain-based ethanol producers and sections of the sugar industry over feedstock pricing, allocation priorities and the potential implications for the sector.

The tender sets procurement prices at ₹60.32 a litre for surplus foodgrains (SFG), with a stated cap of 108 crore litres for the first three quarters; ₹64 a litre for damaged foodgrains (DFG); and ₹66 a litre for maize, plus an additional ₹2.79 a litre. While ethanol produced from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses has been excluded, C-heavy molasses-based ethanol remains eligible for procurement.

The Grain Ethanol Manufacturers Association (GEMA) has argued that the tender places a disproportionate burden on rice-based feedstocks, particularly SFG and DFG, while potentially weakening maize’s role as an industrial feedstock.
The pricing differential has also created uncertainty over how procurement demand will be distributed among the different feedstock categories.

According to industry estimates, DFG-based ethanol allocation during ESY 2025–26 was approximately 60 crore litres. For ESY 2026–27, the industry anticipates that the allocation could exceed 700 crore litres.

C.K. Jain, president of GEMA, said a balanced ethanol policy must support viable production from both maize and rice, with procurement prices reflecting their different cost structures and allocations providing reasonable visibility to producers. He added that the government and OMCs should review the pricing and allocation framework.

GEMA has also questioned whether maize will receive adequate procurement opportunities under the lowest-price-based allocation mechanism. It has called for greater clarity on the methodology for feedstock-wise allocation and the role envisaged for maize in meeting the country’s ethanol requirements.

The Indian Sugar & Bio-Energy Manufacturers Association (ISMA) has welcomed the exclusion of ethanol produced from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses, arguing that the approach is consistent with the need to safeguard domestic sugar availability amid uncertainty over the forthcoming crop.
C-heavy molasses-based ethanol, it noted, allows sugar mills to continue contributing to the ethanol-blending programme without diverting recoverable sugar.
However, ISMA has raised concerns over the preferential allocation granted to dedicated ethanol plants holding Long-Term Offtake Agreements under the ESY 2026–27 tender.
While the provision is already in place for the current year, its continuation in subsequent years could hurt the sugar industry, the association said.

articles.title: Data suggests broad-based increase in food prices: RBI Bulletin
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: High-frequency data collected by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) for October (till 19th), suggest a broad-based increase in food prices, said RBI officials in the October edition of RBI Bulletin, which was released on Friday (October 23, 2026).

“Among cereals, rice and wheat prices continued to increase. Prices of major pulses also went up sequentially. Edible oil prices also recorded a slow and broad-based increase, led by mustard and palm oil,” they wrote in the ‘State of the Economy’ article.
Among vegetables, while potato prices declined and the pace of onion price increases dropped, tomato prices picked up, they added.

Surprisingly, inflation in rural areas has been getting higher than that in urban areas. Inflation stood at 4.9% and 6.1%, respectively, in urban and rural areas in September. In August, urban and rural inflation stood at 4.3% and 5.2% respectively, the officials stated.
ALSO WATCH The battle against inflation is entering a tougher phase: What it means for you

The majority of States/UTs recorded inflation in the range of 4-6% in September. Inflation ranged from 2.9% to 6.9% across states/UTs. States like Telangana, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry recorded inflation in excess of 6% across both rural and urban areas, they pointed out.

Stating that WPI inflation recorded its first double-digit rate in the new series (Base 2022-23) at 11.4% in September 2026, rising from 9.9% in August, reflecting a broad-based increase in prices, they said industrial and farm input costs remained elevated.
Inflation in the Output Producer Price Index surged to 11.4% in September 2026 from 9.8% in August, led by manufacturing products, and mining & quarrying, they said.
As per the article headline, CPI inflation edged up over the months and showed signs of greater generalisation across commodities, calling for a commensurate change in the monetary policy stance.
“The external headwinds are also being dealt with a slew of regulatory measures by the Reserve Bank to curb speculative activity in foreign exchange market,” they stated.

“Strong inflows under FCNR(B) swap window augmented reserves. Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), External Commercial Borrowing (ECB) and remittance flows strengthened in August. With strong exports growth, the trade deficit narrowed in September,” they added.

The headline Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation rose to a 23-month high of 5.5% (YoY) in September from 4.8% in August, driven by a broad-based increase in food, fuel and core (CPI excluding food and fuel) components.

articles.title: Falling short: on Marco Rubio’s second visit to India
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The United States Secretary of State’s three-day visit to India , his second in five months, came at a significant time in U.S. politics. Marco Rubio’s Mumbai trip this week was just ahead of the U.S. midterm elections , which would mark the midpoint of President Donald Trump’s second term in office — a point at which the incumbent normally begins to focus on legacy, and possible contenders for the next Presidential election (Mr. Rubio is expected to be one), and start to look for possible partners and friendships around the world. In addition, his visit also raised hopes in New Delhi of a reset in bilateral ties, battered by two years of uncertainty over the Trump administration’s actions. This would include positive moves towards concluding the Bilateral Trade Agreement , reassuring India about U.S. sanctions on the import of Russian oil, preparations for upcoming Trump meets with Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the Manila (ASEAN) and Miami (G-20) summits, discussing plans for the Quad Summit (on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit) that India has been trying to host, and setting a date for Mr. Trump’s India visit. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar’s invitation also offered Mr. Rubio an opportunity to meet their UAE counterpart, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, to discuss the Gulf situation and to restore energy security and connectivity. And finally, Mr. Rubio’s visit to the Jamnagar Reliance refinery, led to speculation of some major deals on energy, possibly offering more discounts as he pitched for India to buy more American and U.S.-licensed Venezuelan oil.

Given all the high expectations, the visit was bound to come up short. The optics of his visit to Mumbai and Jamnagar, but not New Delhi, which was announced by the U.S. Ambassador to India , gave the Opposition fodder to question the real purpose of the visit. Despite Mr. Rubio’s two visits to India and more than six by Mr. Jaishankar to the U.S. since Mr. Trump took office, relations remain on edge, with issues on trade, tariffs, H-1B restrictions and anti-immigrant measures unaddressed. Also, the U.S.’s narrative on Operation Sindoor (2025), growing ties with Pakistan, and the Trump administration’s rhetoric on India’s economy, diaspora and Russian oil trade have added to India’s unhappiness. The two sides did not announce any agreements and Mr. Jaishankar and Mr. Rubio did not hold a joint press address. However, as they did at the U.S. Independence Day’s 250th anniversary celebrations in Delhi in May, they attended the “Freedom 250” event in Mumbai. Mr. Rubio acknowledged that while no two countries would agree on all issues, he said the U.S.-India alignment on core issues of national interest was “extraordinary” . From this point on, Mr. Rubio must walk that talk, with a view to ensuring that India-U.S. ties are able to move on from the difficulties of the last few years.

articles.title: In the crossfire: on India and the Saudi-Houthi conflict
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The killing of an Indian national in a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Dammam airport is a grim reminder of the dangers the kingdom’s Indian community faces as the conflict between Riyadh and Yemen’s Shia militants escalates. Since the fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis resumed in July, at least two Indians have been killed and 14 others wounded. On Thursday, the Houthis claimed that a yacht with 14 Indians was targeted by Saudi forces near Yemen’s Zuqar island in the Red Sea and that rescue operations were under way. As the Houthis, who control parts of Northern Yemen and its entire Red Sea coast, step up attacks on Saudi infrastructure, including oil facilities and airports, Indians, who are the kingdom’s largest expat community, risk getting caught in the crossfire. With flights disrupted, thousands of Indian pilgrims are stranded. India has condemned Houthi attacks, saying that it “stands in solidarity” with Saudi Arabia. With no end in sight to the fighting and a high possibility of Israel and the U.S. resuming their Iran strikes, further violence and instability in West Asia could make India’s choices increasingly difficult.

The Saudi-Houthi conflict dates back to the Houthi takeover of Sana’a, Yemen’s capital, in 2014. A year later, Saudi Arabia began bombing Yemen to drive the Houthis out. But years of Saudi bombing of one of the poorest Arab countries have proved counterproductive; the Houthis consolidated support among the tribes of northern Yemen and built a powerful territorial army and naval force. The Saudi-Houthi ceasefire of 2022 collapsed in July 2026 after Saudi Arabia recklessly bombed Sana’a airport, to prevent an Iranian plane with a Houthi delegation from landing. The Houthis subsequently began attacking Saudi Arabia’s critical infrastructure, and launched a ground offensive against the Saudi-backed forces in Yemen. The Houthi attacks pose the biggest security challenge to Mohammed bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince and the main architect of the war on Yemen, in decades. Massive Saudi air strikes have neither defeated the Houthis nor restored the kingdom’s deterrence. With its wealth, natural resources, infrastructure and tenuous palace politics, the kingdom remains exposed to Houthi missile and drone attacks, with few good options for a way out. India must prepare a contingency plan for worst-case scenarios. Its immediate priority should be to evacuate stranded Indian pilgrims. It should also articulate a stronger position for stability and work with Arab countries and Tehran to push for a diplomatic settlement to the Iran crisis . For peace to prevail in the Persian Gulf, the guns directed at Iran must first fall silent.
